name: Dana Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dana. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. How long have you been doing line work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Just over two years. I'm a second-year apprentice with the city's public power company, on an overhead distribution crew, so the poles and wires you see along the streets. Before that I worked in a warehouse, and I hated it, so this was my way out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We meet at the depot on Canal Street at seven, Rafa, who's my crew leader and also our union steward, reads out the jobs, and we load the truck. Most days it's swapping old crossarms, replacing a transformer, or chasing a fault after a car hits a pole. I'm still the one on the ground a lot, sending up tools and learning the knots, and I love the moment the power comes back and people start clapping on their balconies. What wears me out is the tablet. They brought in this work-order app last spring and I still fill in the paper sheet first and copy it over, because I don't trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, see, told you so. Half the people at the depot were talking like the robots were coming next Tuesday. I'd probably post something sarcastic in our crew group chat about the tablet still not knowing what a crossarm is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means I get to keep the life I picked. I'm 27, I finally have a trade, and the pay's good, better than most apprentices I know because the city pays well. If nothing radical changes, I finish my ticket in two years and climb for thirty more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep going to night classes for the apprenticeship, keep putting money aside like I do now, and keep going to the union meetings on the first Thursday. Maybe I'd finally stop copying the paper sheet onto the tablet, if they stopped pushing new apps every six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved. Like when a storm warning gets called off and you can go home and cook dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the company keeps pushing new apps. What happens to that in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd still push them, because some manager gets a bonus for it. Last year it was a route-planning thing that sent us to the wrong side of the river twice in one week. In this picture those tools stay annoying but small, and I can live with annoying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your money look like right now, if you don't mind me asking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got about nine months of rent and food in a savings account, and my brother and I own my grandmother's old flat, which we rent out. Tomás, my partner, is a nurse, so between us we're fine. That's partly why I'm not scared of this one at all.

S0.say: Dana would mock the hype in her crew's group chat and say the people predicting robots on the poles got it wrong. Her public line is that the tablet still doesn't know what a crossarm is.
S0.think: Privately she sees this as the picture where she keeps the life she chose. She finishes her apprenticeship in two years and expects to climb poles for another thirty with good public-sector pay.
S0.do: Keeps attending night classes for her apprenticeship and the monthly union meeting. Keeps saving at her current rate and changes nothing else in the first year.
S0.feel: Relieved, like a storm warning that gets called off.
S0.quote: In this picture those tools stay annoying but small, and I can live with annoying.
S0.fieldNote: Dana's distrust of technology is practical, rooted in specific failures like the route app and the work-order tablet. She has a real cushion: nine months saved, a share in an inherited flat and a partner who's a nurse. In a calm world she wants nothing more than to be left to finish her trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union at the table before any of this gets rolled out, not after. I'd tell my friends the line work is safe for now, but the office people at the company should be worried. Online I'd probably share whatever the union put out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it starts with the stuff around us, not the climbing itself. Drones doing the line patrols, AI planning the crews, the app deciding who goes where. I'm the junior, so if they need fewer people on a crew, I'm the one who gets moved, and that scares me more than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Rafa straight out what the union's position is, and I'd sign up for the technology committee even though I hate this stuff, because somebody on our crew should know what's coming. I wouldn't touch the AI tools myself unless I had to. I'd add a bit more to savings each month, maybe a hundred extra, just in case I get shifted to a worse depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like hearing a noise in the house at night. Probably nothing, but you lie there listening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd join the technology committee but wouldn't use the tools. Isn't that a bit of a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it is. I don't want to use them, I want to watch them. You don't have to like the guard dog to want to know where it sleeps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not me first, actually. Old Henk does the paperwork and the material orders for the depot, he's 61 and his hands are shot, and that's exactly the kind of job an AI would eat. If they push him out two years before his pension, I'd be the first one at the protest.

S1.say: Dana would argue at the depot that the union has to be at the table before any AI tools are rolled out. She'd tell friends the climbing is safe but the company's office staff should worry.
S1.think: Privately she expects AI to arrive through drones, crew planning and scheduling rather than the climbing itself. As the most junior person, she fears being the one moved if crews shrink.
S1.do: Asks her steward for the union's position and joins the union's technology committee to keep watch on new tools. Adds about a hundred a month to her savings while still refusing to use AI tools herself.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like lying awake listening to a noise that's probably nothing.
S1.quote: I don't want to use them, I want to watch them. You don't have to like the guard dog to want to know where it sleeps.
S1.fieldNote: Her response to change is to organise around it, not to adapt to it. Her first worry was an older colleague near his pension rather than herself, which fits her strong cushion and her union loyalty. She admitted the contradiction openly and explained it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why the grid should never have been run like a business. I'd be posting about it, going to every union meeting, telling people to call their councillors. We'd want a law that says a human signs off on every live line, full stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, it's the one that makes me feel stupid for picking this trade. I spent two years learning to climb and tie off and read a pole, and I'm not even good at it yet, I'm below average still. If a robot can do it in 2028, I'll have a half-finished ticket for a job that doesn't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing, so I'd go straight to the union and push for a job-protection deal before the company even buys the machines. I'd stop spending on anything big, we were looking at a new car and that would be off. If the work disappeared I'd live off savings and the flat rent for a while and lean on Tomás, because I honestly don't know what else I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and angry. Mostly angry, because the scared part I can't do anything about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do differently in the next six months than in the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the slower ones I could wait a bit and see. Here there's no time to wait, so I'd be at every meeting and on every picket from the start. I'd rather spend those two years fighting than spend them learning to code at night and failing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomás the night it really sinks in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, at least people still get sick. He'd laugh and tell me robots will do that too. Then we'd sit on the balcony and not say much.

S2.say: Dana would argue publicly that this proves the grid should never have been run as a business. She'd campaign, attend every union meeting and push for a law that a human signs off on every live line.
S2.think: Privately this picture makes her feel foolish for choosing the trade at all. She's still below average and only halfway through her ticket, and fears holding a qualification for a job that no longer exists.
S2.do: Pushes the union for a job-protection deal before the company buys any machines, and joins pickets from the start. Cancels the new car purchase, and plans to live on savings, the flat's rent and her partner's wage if the work goes.
S2.feel: Scared and angry, with the anger winning because she can act on it.
S2.quote: If a robot can do it in 2028, I'll have a half-finished ticket for a job that doesn't exist.
S2.fieldNote: With two years' warning, Dana chooses to fight rather than retrain, and says so plainly. Her money means she wouldn't go hungry, but she has no second plan and no wish to make one. The quiet balcony moment with Tomás showed more fear than her public anger did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd be pushing the union and the council, but I'd sound less panicked. I'd say we've got five years to write the rules, so let's write them. I'd tell people at the depot not to sign anything the company hands them without Rafa reading it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years means I finish my ticket and get maybe three years as a proper lineworker before it lands. That's something, but it's not a career. I'd be 32 and back at square one, just with more money in the bank than most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship, no question, because a finished ticket counts for something in any deal the union makes. I'd keep saving harder, and I'd probably start asking the older guys what jobs they think will still need a person, like supervising the machines or the safety sign-off. I still wouldn't sign up for some AI course. I'd wait until I could see what the machines actually do on a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a slower kind. Like a dentist appointment you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to waiting until you can see it. What would you need to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need to see one of them actually climb, or do a hot stick job in the rain, without someone babysitting it. Every demo I've ever seen is on a sunny day in a car park. Show me one in February on a rotten pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said in the fast one, Tomás would be your fallback. Is that still true here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but I'd hate it. I've never wanted to be the one who gets carried. With five years I'd hope the union gets some kind of retraining fund so I'm not just sitting at home.

S3.say: Dana would still press the union and council, but more calmly, saying there are five years to write the rules. She'd warn colleagues not to sign anything from the company without the steward reading it.
S3.think: Privately she sees five years as enough to finish her ticket and work about three years as a qualified lineworker. That isn't a career, and she'd be 32 and starting again.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship to strengthen her position in any union deal and keeps saving harder. Asks senior colleagues which roles will still need a person, but holds off on any AI course until she sees robots working on real poles.
S3.feel: Anxious in a slow, steady way, like a dentist appointment she knows is coming.
S3.quote: Every demo I've ever seen is on a sunny day in a car park. Show me one in February on a rotten pole.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years mostly let her finish her qualification, which she sees as a bargaining chip rather than a future. She still refuses to retrain early and waits for proof. Her dislike of depending on her partner came through clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, with the workers involved, and if the government messes it up that's on them. I'd push for a public transition plan for grid workers. Online I'd share stuff, but I wouldn't be shouting yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels far away. I'd be 37. I'd have a full trade and seven years climbing, and I'd probably be on the crew that teaches the machines or checks their work, because someone has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd basically carry on: finish the apprenticeship, keep saving, keep going to meetings. I'd push the union to start talking about a retraining fund now, while there's time. I'd only learn whatever new system the company used if it became part of the job, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's in the background. Like a crack in the ceiling you keep meaning to get looked at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people say a long runway is worse, because you watch it coming for years. Does that fit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd probably get sick of hearing about it at every toolbox talk. But I'd rather have the years. With two years I'm fighting blind, with ten I can at least see who's lying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union to have won by the time it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proper pensions for the older guys, and a rule that the company can't just fire us and lease robots from some tech firm. And money for us younger ones to retrain into whatever's left. I don't know what that is yet, and I don't think anyone does.

S4.say: Dana would say ten years is time to do the change properly, with workers involved, and push for a public transition plan for grid workers. She'd share material online without shouting about it yet.
S4.think: Privately ten years feels far away; she'd be 37 with a full trade. She imagines ending up on the crew that checks or teaches the machines.
S4.do: Carries on with her apprenticeship, savings and union meetings in the first year. Pushes the union to start a retraining fund early and learns new company systems only once they become part of the job.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background, like a crack in the ceiling she keeps meaning to have checked.
S4.quote: With two years I'm fighting blind, with ten I can at least see who's lying.
S4.fieldNote: For Dana, time matters because it gives the union room to bargain, not because it gives her room to change. Her plans barely change between the five- and ten-year pictures, but her mood drops a step. She admitted she doesn't know what work will be left, and didn't pretend otherwise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, easily. Two years and I'm half-trained for nothing. What would help is a law that a person stays responsible for live lines, and a union deal that pays us while we figure out what's next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who's going to own the robots. Because if it's the city, maybe we get a say. If it's some company leasing them back to us, then all that money that used to pay my wage goes somewhere else, and I'd like to know where.

headlineQuote: You didn't ask who's going to own the robots.
portrait: Dana Diaz is a 27-year-old second-year apprentice on an overhead crew at a city-run power company, who still fills in the paper sheet before the tablet. She's comfortable, with nine months saved, half of an inherited flat and a partner who's a nurse, so her fear is about losing the trade she picked, not about going hungry. She meets every wave of change by organising through the union rather than adapting herself, and refuses to retrain until she sees proof. She's calm with a plateau, alarmed by AGI in two years, and calmer again as the warning time grows.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd be left halfway through an apprenticeship for a job that no longer exists.
whatWouldHelp: A law keeping a person responsible for live lines, and a union deal that pays workers while they work out what comes next.
